etymology: Greek demos, the people, and kratos, rule. Webster (1828) gives it as “Gr. People, and to possess, to govern.”
biblical_def: Democracy is government by the people. Webster (1828) defines it as “a form of government, in which the supreme power is lodged in the hands of the people collectively, or in which the people exercise the powers of legislation,” and gives one example: “Such was the government of Athens.” He keeps it distinct from a republic, where that power is exercised by elected representatives. Scripture does not name the form, but it speaks plainly to the people as a power in the state. Moses told the tribes, “Take you wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes, and I will make them rulers over you” (Deu 1:13): the people chose, and God’s law set the standard. The same people could choose against God. When Israel demanded a king, the LORD told Samuel, “they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me” (1Sa 8:7), and still “the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel” (1Sa 8:19). The voice of the many is not the voice of God. The law forbids it outright: “Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil” (Exo 23:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DEMOCRACY, government by the people; the supreme power lodged in the people collectively, as at Athens.
webster_full: DEMOCRACY, noun [Gr. People, and to possess, to govern.] Government by the people; a form of government, in which the supreme power is lodged in the hands of the people collectively, or in which the people exercise the powers of legislation. Such was the government of Athens.
corruption_summary: Modern usage makes democracy a moral end in itself, so that whatever a majority wills is counted right.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster defined democracy as a form of government, a way of lodging power. Today the word is used as if it named a virtue, and whatever is called democratic is assumed to be just. But a form of government cannot make a law righteous. Israel’s demand for a king was the people’s own voice, and God called it a rejection of Himself (1Sa 8:7).

The word is also used loosely for any government with elections, which erases the distinction Webster drew between a democracy and a republic. A people that rules itself is still under God, and “Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil” (Exo 23:2) binds the many as much as the one.

etymology: Latin respublica, from res, thing or affair, and publica, public. Webster (1828): “respublica; res and publica; public affairs.”
biblical_def: A republic is a commonwealth governed by elected representatives. Webster (1828) defines it as “a state in which the exercise of the sovereign power is lodged in representatives elected by the people,” and adds that “in modern usage, it differs from a democracy or democratic state, in which the people exercise the powers of sovereignty in person.” Scripture gives the pattern of chosen rulers bound by a standard above them. Jethro counselled Moses to “provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness” (Exo 18:21). Moses told the tribes to choose “wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes” (Deu 1:13), and the law required that judges “shall judge the people with just judgment” (Deu 16:18). However rulers are chosen, their power is not their own: “there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): REPUBLIC, a commonwealth; a state in which the sovereign power is exercised by representatives elected by the people.
webster_full: REPUB'LIC, noun [Latin respublica; res and publica; public affairs.]

1. A commonwealth; a state in which the exercise of the sovereign power is lodged in representatives elected by the people. In modern usage, it differs from a democracy or democratic state, in which the people exercise the powers of sovereignty in person. Yet the democracies of Greece are often called republics.
2. Common interest; the public. [Not in use.]
Republic of letters, the collective body of learned men.
corruption_summary: The word is now used for almost any state without a king, and the distinction from democracy that Webster drew is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster gave republic a precise meaning: power exercised by elected representatives, not by the people in person. Modern speech blurs the two and calls nearly every state a republic or a democracy without distinction. The loss matters, because representation was meant to restrain the passions of the many.

The deeper error is to think that elected rulers answer only to those who elected them. Exo 18:21 asks first for men “such as fear God,” and Rom 13:1 says the powers are “ordained of God.” Representatives answer to God before they answer to voters.

pos: n. phrase (a written declaration of rights)
etymology: English bill, a written paper, and right, a just claim. Webster (1828) has no separate headword for the phrase; he defines it under BILL, sense 14.
biblical_def: A bill of rights is a written summary of the rights a people claim against their rulers. Webster (1828) defines the phrase under BILL: “A bill of rights is a summary of rights and privileges, claimed by a people. Such was the declaration presented by the lords and commons of England to the prince and princess of Orange in 1688.” He adds that in America such a declaration “is prefixed to most of the constitutions of the several states.” Scripture does not use the phrase, but it does put rulers under a written law. The king of Israel was to “write him a copy of this law in a book” (Deu 17:18), and Samuel “told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and laid it up before the LORD” (1Sa 10:25). The law also guarded the weak in court: “Thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor in his cause” (Exo 23:6); “thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift” (Deu 16:19). And God pronounced woe on rulers “that decree unrighteous decrees” (Isa 10:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under BILL, sense 14: a bill of rights is a summary of rights and privileges, claimed by a people.
webster_full: BILL, noun (sense 14)

14. A bill of rights is a summary of rights and privileges, claimed by a people. Such was the declaration presented by the lords and commons of England to the prince and princess of Orange in 1688. In America, a bill or declaration or rights is prefixed to most of the constitutions of the several states.
corruption_summary: Rights are now often treated as grants of the state, or as any want a person can claim, rather than just claims protected by law.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster defined a bill of rights as rights “claimed by a people” against their rulers. The 1688 declaration and the American state declarations set limits on power. Modern usage often reverses this, treating rights as whatever the state chooses to grant and may take back.

A second corruption stretches rights to cover every desire. A right, in Webster, is a just claim. Scripture’s protections are concrete: just judgment for the poor, no respect of persons, no bribes (Exo 23:6; Deu 16:19). Rulers who write unjust decrees stand under God’s woe (Isa 10:1).

etymology: From prelate, Latin praelatus, set before. Webster (1828): “from prelate.”
biblical_def: Prelacy is the office of a prelate, and by extension church government by a ruling order of bishops set over other ministers. Webster (1828) gives “the office or dignity of a prelate,” then “episcopacy; the order of bishops,” and “bishops, collectively.” He quotes the old protest against those “that call themselves protestants, who put prelacy and popery together as terms convertible.” The question prelacy raises is whether Christ set lords over His church. He answered it Himself: “Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them”, “But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” (Mat 20:25-26). Peter, an elder writing to elders, forbids ruling “as being lords over God’s heritage” (1Pe 5:3). Paul told the Ephesian elders that the Holy Ghost had made them “overseers, to feed the church of God” (Act 20:28), and John warned against Diotrephes, “who loveth to have the preeminence among them” (3Jn 1:9).

corruption_summary: Prelacy is now an unfamiliar word, and the debate it names, whether bishops rule over other ministers by divine right, is often forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: In Webster’s day prelacy was a live word in the debates over church government. Presbyterians and Independents used it of a hierarchy of bishops ruling over presbyters. Now the word has nearly dropped out of use, and with it the question whether the New Testament gives one order of minister authority over another.

Webster’s own quotation shows the older Protestant fear: that prelacy and popery would become “terms convertible.” Whatever polity a church holds, the standard is Christ’s word: “it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26). Elders are to be ensamples, not lords (1Pe 5:3).

pos: n. (one who instructs by question and answer)
etymology: Greek katecheo, to instruct by word of mouth, through Latin catechista. Webster (1828) enters CATECHIST without an etymology note.
biblical_def: A catechist is a teacher of the first principles of the faith. Webster (1828) defines him as one who instructs “by question and answer; a catechiser; one appointed by the church to instruct in the principles of religion.” Scripture places teaching at the center of the life of God’s people. Parents were the first catechists: “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house” (Deu 6:7). Luke wrote so that Theophilus “mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4). Apollos “was instructed in the way of the Lord” (Act 18:25). And the one taught owes the teacher: “Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things” (Gal 6:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CATECHIST, one who instructs by question and answer; a catechiser; one appointed by the church to instruct in the principles of religion.
webster_full: CATECHIST, noun One who instructs viva voice, or by question and answer; a catechiser; one appointed by the church to instruct in the principles of religion.
corruption_summary: Catechizing is often treated as rote memory work for children, or dropped, so that churches no longer appoint anyone to teach first principles.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s catechist was “appointed by the church.” The office assumed that believers must be taught the principles of religion in order, by question and answer. Many churches have let that office go, leaving instruction to sermons alone or to nothing.

Where catechizing survives it is sometimes dismissed as rote recitation. But Deu 6:7 puts teaching into the whole of daily life, and Luk 1:4 ties instruction to certainty. The goal is understanding, not only memory.

pos: n. (one who confesses Christ; one who hears confession)
etymology: Latin confessor, from confiteor, to acknowledge. Webster (1828) enters CONFESS’OR with three senses.
biblical_def: A confessor is first one who confesses. Webster (1828) gives three senses: “one who confesses; one who acknowledges his sins”; “one who makes a profession of his faith in the Christian religion,” used especially of “one who avows his religion in the face of danger, and adheres to it, in defiance of persecution and torture”; and “a priest; one who hears the confessions of others, and has power to grant them absolution.” The second sense is the scriptural one. Christ Himself “before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession” (1Ti 6:13), and Timothy had “professed a good profession before many witnesses” (1Ti 6:12). The promise is: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32). At Pergamos the church held fast Christ’s name “even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr” (Rev 2:13). Scripture gives no priest power to absolve; God alone forgives sins, through Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CONFESSOR, one who acknowledges his sins; one who professes the Christian faith, especially in the face of persecution; a priest who hears confessions.
webster_full: CONFESS'OR, noun
1. One who confesses; one who acknowledges his sins.

2. One who makes a profession of his faith in the Christian religion. The word is appropriately used to denote one who avows his religion in the face of danger, and adheres to it, in defiance of persecution and torture. It was formerly used as synonymous with martyr; afterwards it was applied to those who, having been persecuted and tormented, were permitted to die in peace. It was used also for such Christians as lived a good life, and died with the reputation of sanctity.
3. A priest; one who hears the confessions of others, and has power to grant them absolution.
corruption_summary: The word now usually means a priest who hears confession, and the older sense of a believer who confesses Christ under persecution is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster puts the priest last. His fullest sense is the believer “who avows his religion in the face of danger.” Modern usage has reversed the order, so that a confessor is assumed to be a cleric in a booth. That shift hides the Bible’s use, in which every believer is called to confess Christ before men (Mat 10:32).

The third sense carries a claim Scripture does not make: that a priest “has power to grant” absolution. Believers confess their faults one to another and pray, but forgiveness belongs to God through the one Mediator.

pos: n. (a supposed sign of a future event)
etymology: Latin omen. Webster (1828) gives “Latin omen; Heb. an augur.”
biblical_def: An omen is an event taken as a sign of what is to come. Webster (1828) defines it as “a sign or indication of some future event; a prognostic,” and passes judgment in the same entry: “Superstition and ignorance multiply omens; philosophy and truth reject all omens, except such as may be called causes of the events.” He asks, “Without a miracle, how can one event be the omen of another with which it has no connection?” Scripture forbids the practice of reading omens. Israel was not to “use enchantment, nor observe times” (Lev 19:26), and among them was not to be found any one that “useth divination, or an observer of times” (Deu 18:10). Manasseh “observed times, and used enchantments”, and so “wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD” (2Ki 21:6). God said, “Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven” (Jer 10:2), for He is the one “That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad” (Isa 44:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): OMEN, a sign or indication of some future event; a prognostic. Superstition multiplies omens; truth rejects them.
webster_full: O'MEN, noun [Latin omen; Heb. an augur.]

A sign or indication of some future event; a prognostic. Superstition and ignorance multiply omens; philosophy and truth reject all omens, except such as may be called causes of the events. Without a miracle, how can one event be the omen of another with which it has no connection?
corruption_summary: Omen is now used casually, as a harmless figure of speech or as entertainment, and the practice Scripture forbids is treated as play.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster did not treat omens as neutral. He said superstition and ignorance multiply them, and truth rejects them. Today omens are a stock device of film and games, and many people still watch for signs in dates, numbers and coincidences without thinking of it as divination.

Scripture names the observer of times among the practices God abhors (Deu 18:10). The believer is told not to be “dismayed at the signs of heaven” (Jer 10:2), because the future is in God’s hand, not written in chance events.

etymology: Latin augurium, from augur, a Roman diviner. Webster (1828): “Latin augurium.”
biblical_def: Augury is the art of foretelling events from signs. Webster (1828) defines it first as “the art or practice of foretelling events by the flight or chattering of birds,” and second as “an omen; prediction; prognostication.” The Roman augur read birds; other nations read stars, arrows, and the entrails of sacrifices. Scripture describes the king of Babylon who “stood at the parting of the way, at the head of the two ways, to use divination: he made his arrows bright, he consulted with images, he looked in the liver” (Eze 21:21). God mocked Babylon’s “astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators” (Isa 47:13). Israel was forbidden to “use enchantment, nor observe times” (Lev 19:26), and “There shall not be found among you any one” who “useth divination” (Deu 18:10). God’s people seek the future from His word, not from signs in nature.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): AUGURY, the art or practice of foretelling events by the flight or chattering of birds; an omen, prediction.
webster_full: AU'GURY, noun [Latin augurium.]
1. The art or practice of foretelling events by the flight or chattering of birds.
2. An omen; prediction; prognostication.
corruption_summary: Augury now survives mainly as a literary word for any forecast, which hides its origin in pagan divination.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s first sense is the Roman practice of reading birds. Modern writers use augury loosely for any sign or forecast, as in “an augury of success,” and the pagan root is forgotten.

The practice itself has not disappeared; it has changed its signs. Horoscopes and the search for signs in events serve the same desire to know the future apart from God. Isa 47:13 shows what such counsellors can do: they cannot save.

etymology: Latin amuletum. Webster (1828): “Latin amuletum; amolior, amolitus to remove.”
biblical_def: An amulet is a charm worn for protection. Webster (1828) defines it as “something worn as a remedy or preservative against evils or mischief, such as diseases and witchcraft,” made of “certain stones, metals or plants; sometimes of words, characters or sentences, arranged in a particular order.” He notes they “were appended to the neck or body.” Scripture treats trust in such objects as idolatry. When Jacob called his household back to God, “they gave unto Jacob all the strange gods which were in their hand, and all their earrings which were in their ears; and Jacob hid them under the oak which was by Shechem” (Gen 35:4). Ezekiel pronounced woe on the women who made coverings “to hunt souls” (Eze 13:18). At Ephesus, those “which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men” (Act 19:19), though the price came to “fifty thousand pieces of silver”. The Christian’s protection is the Lord, not an object.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): AMULET, something worn as a remedy or preservative against evils or mischief, such as diseases and witchcraft.
webster_full: AM'ULET, noun [Latin amuletum; amolior, amolitus to remove.]

Something worn as a remedy or preservative against evils or mischief, such as diseases and witchcraft. Amulets, in days of ignorance, were common. They consisted of certain stones, metals or plants; sometimes of words, characters or sentences, arranged in a particular order. They were appended to the neck or body. Among some nations, they are still in use.
corruption_summary: Amulets are now sold as jewelry or lucky charms and treated as harmless, while the trust they express is the same Webster described.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster wrote that amulets “in days of ignorance, were common,” and that “among some nations, they are still in use.” Today they are marketed as jewelry, crystals and lucky tokens, often with no thought of what they claim to do. The claim is still that an object can ward off evil.

Even sacred words can be made into amulets when a verse or symbol is worn as a charm rather than believed. Scripture’s pattern is the Ephesian bonfire (Act 19:19): such things are given up, not kept for luck.

pos: n. (a supposed region bordering on hell)
etymology: Latin limbus, a border or hem. Webster (1828) enters LIM’BO and LIM’BUS together: “Latin limbus.”
biblical_def: Limbo is the name given in Roman Catholic teaching to a supposed border region of the dead. Webster (1828) defines it as “a region bordering on hell, or hell itself,” adding: “Among catholics, a place where the souls of persons are lodged after death.” His second sense is general: “a place of restraint.” Scripture knows no such border place. It speaks of a fixed division after death: “between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot” (Luk 16:26). “it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27). For the believer, to be “absent from the body” is “to be present with the Lord” (2Co 5:8). Christ told the dying thief, “To day shalt thou be with me in paradise” (Luk 23:43), and Paul desired “to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better” (Php 1:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): LIMBO, a region bordering on hell, or hell itself; among Catholics, a place where souls are lodged after death; a place of restraint.
webster_full: LIM'BO,
LIM'BUS, noun [Latin limbus.]
1. A region bordering on hell, or hell itself.
Among catholics, a place where the souls of persons are lodged after death.
2. A place of restraint.
corruption_summary: Limbo is now chiefly a figure of speech for being stuck or undecided, and its origin as an unbiblical doctrine of the afterlife is forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s second sense, “a place of restraint,” has become the main one: a project or a person “in limbo” is waiting on a decision. The theological claim behind the word, that souls are lodged in a border region after death, passes unnoticed.

That claim has no ground in Scripture. The Bible speaks of a great gulf fixed (Luk 16:26), of judgment after death (Heb 9:27), and of believers present with the Lord (2Co 5:8). It gives no third place in between.

etymology: From mis-, wrongly, and Latin credens, believing. Webster (1828): “Latin credens, credo.”
biblical_def: A miscreant was first an unbeliever. Webster (1828) gives two senses: “an infidel, or one who embraces a false faith,” and “a vile wretch; an unprincipled fellow.” The word moved from the first to the second because men saw that false belief and corrupt life go together. Scripture draws the line between belief and unbelief sharply: “what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?” (2Co 6:15). It also measures faith by conduct: whoever will not provide for his own “hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel” (1Ti 5:8). Some “profess that they know God; but in works they deny him” (Tit 1:16). Proverbs describes the man Webster’s second sense names: “A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth” (Pro 6:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MISCREANT, an infidel, or one who embraces a false faith; a vile wretch, an unprincipled fellow.
webster_full: MIS'CREANT, noun [Latin credens, credo.]
1. An infidel, or one who embraces a false faith.
2. A vile wretch; an unprincipled fellow.
corruption_summary: Miscreant now means only a petty wrongdoer, and the older sense of one who holds a false faith has dropped away.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster put the religious sense first. A miscreant was an infidel, one who embraces a false faith. Today the word is used half in jest for a troublemaker or vandal, and nobody hears its root in credo, I believe.

The shift hides a connection Scripture keeps: belief and life go together. One who denies God in works is reckoned with the unbeliever (Tit 1:16), and one who neglects his own house is “worse than an infidel” (1Ti 5:8).

etymology: Greek dioikesis, administration, through Latin dioecesis. Webster (1828) glosses the Greek as “administration, a province or jurisdiction.”
biblical_def: A diocese is the territory under a bishop’s authority. Webster (1828) defines it as “the circuit or extent of a bishops jurisdiction; an ecclesiastical division of a kingdom or state, subject to the authority of a bishop.” He notes that “a diocese was originally a division of the Roman empire for the purpose of civil government, a prefecture. But the term is now exclusively appropriated to ecclesiastical jurisdiction.” The word is not in Scripture, and the New Testament pattern is plural oversight in each local church. Paul left Titus in Crete to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). Paul and Barnabas “ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23). From Miletus Paul “called the elders of the church” of Ephesus (Act 20:17) and told them the Holy Ghost had made them “overseers, to feed the church of God” (Act 20:28). Peter charged elders: “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DIOCESE, the circuit or extent of a bishop’s jurisdiction; an ecclesiastical division subject to a bishop; originally a Roman civil division.
webster_full: DIOCESE, noun [Gr., administration, a province or jurisdiction; residence; to dwell; a house. diocese is a very erroneous orthography.] The circuit or extent of a bishops jurisdiction; an ecclesiastical division of a kingdom or state, subject to the authority of a bishop. In England there are two provinces or circuits of archbishops jurisdiction, Canterbury and York. The province of Canterbury contains twenty-one dioceses, and that of York three, besides the isle of Man. Every diocese is divided into archdeaconries, of which there are sixty; and each archdeaconry, into rural deaneries; and every deanery, into parishes. A diocese was originally a division of the Roman empire for the purpose of civil government, a prefecture. But the term is now exclusively appropriated to ecclesiastical jurisdiction.
corruption_summary: Diocese is now assumed to be a biblical unit of the church, though Webster records that it began as a civil division of the Roman empire.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster is plain about the history: a diocese “was originally a division of the Roman empire for the purpose of civil government.” The church borrowed the empire’s map. Many now speak of the diocese as if it were a New Testament institution.

The New Testament speaks of elders “in every church” (Act 14:23) and “in every city” (Tit 1:5), each body overseen by its own elders. Whatever regional ties churches keep, the flock is fed by elders who are “among” it (1Pe 5:2).

pos: n. (a local church district or society)
etymology: Low Latin parochia, from Greek. Webster (1828) weighs two Greek roots, one meaning a dwelling near, the other an allowance for support, and judges the second more probable.
biblical_def: A parish is a local church and its district. Webster (1828) defines it as “the precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct, the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.” In America he records a different use: “an ecclesiastical society not bounded by territorial limits,” adding, “This is particularly the case in Massachusetts.” Scripture’s unit is the local church in a place. Paul wrote “Unto the church of God which is at Corinth” (1Co 1:2), and greeted “the church that is in their house” (Rom 16:5). Elders were ordained “in every church” (Act 14:23), and they “watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17). The charge to them is local: “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PARISH, the precinct of a secular priest, or whose inhabitants belong to the same church; in America, an ecclesiastical society not bounded by territory.
webster_full: PAR'ISH, noun [Low Latin parochia; Gr. a dwelling or near residence; near, and house, or to dwell; or more probably from the Gr. a salary or largess, an allowance for support; to afford, yield or supply, whence Latin parocha, entertainment given to embassadors at the public expense. If parish is to be deduced from either of these sources, it is probably from the latter, and parish is equivalent to benefice, living, as prebend, from Latin proebeo.
1. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct, the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.

2. In some of the American states, parish is an ecclesiastical society not bounded by territorial limits; but the inhabitants of a town belonging to one church, though residing promiscuously among the people belonging to another church, are called a parish This is particularly the case in Massachusetts. In Connecticut, the legal appellation of such a society is ecclesiastical society.
PAR'ISH, adjective Belonging to a parish; having the spiritual charge of the inhabitants belonging to the same church; as a parish priest.
1. Belonging to a parish; as a parish church; parish records.
2. Maintained by the parish; as parish poor.
corruption_summary: Parish has come to mean a mere administrative district, and the pastoral charge it once carried, a shepherd answerable for the souls in a place, is often forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s adjective sense keeps the old weight: a parish priest has “the spiritual charge of the inhabitants belonging to the same church.” In some places parish now names only a unit of local government, and even in churches it can mean a building and a budget.
Scripture keeps the charge. Those who rule “watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17). A local church is a flock with shepherds who know it, not only an address.

etymology: Greek anti, against, pais, a child, and baptizo, to baptize. Webster (1828): “Gr. against, a child, and baptize.”
biblical_def: An antipedobaptist is one who rejects the baptism of infants. Webster (1828) defines him as “one who is opposed to the baptism of infants.” The word names one side of a long debate among Protestants. Those who baptize only professing believers point to texts that join baptism to faith: “He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved” (Mar 16:16); “when they believed Philip preaching” “they were baptized, both men and women” (Act 8:12). Those who baptize the children of believers point to the promise that follows Peter’s call, “For the promise is unto you, and to your children” (Act 2:39), and to household baptisms, as when the jailer “was baptized, he and all his, straightway” (Act 16:33). Both sides confess that baptism signifies union with Christ: “Buried with him in baptism” (Col 2:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ANTIPEDOBAPTIST, one who is opposed to the baptism of infants.
webster_full: ANTIPEDOBAP'TIST, noun [Gr. against, a child, and baptize.]
One who is opposed to the baptism of infants.
corruption_summary: Antipedobaptist has fallen out of use, and the label is sometimes used as a slur or confused with Anabaptist, a different and older movement.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s term is exact: it describes a position on one question, the baptism of infants. Today the word is rare, and people who hold the position call themselves credobaptists or Baptists. When the old label survives it is sometimes run together with Anabaptist, though the two words do not mean the same thing.

The debate is a real one among those who confess the same gospel, and it turns on how the promise “unto you, and to your children” (Act 2:39) relates to the call to “Repent, and be baptized” (Act 2:38). It should be argued from Scripture, not settled by labels.
